value: fewer flying adult Manx shearwaters over the colony during experimental light-on periods, with a stronger effect under green and blue than under red light; the abstract also gives stronger effects at higher intensity and longer light-on periods
units: categorical (change in number of birds in flight)
eye: adult birds in flight, whole animal
method: field experiment on Skomer Island, Wales: a torch with gel filters (blue, green, red, dimmed white, bright white) placed next to a thermal camera, one minute light-on and one minute light-off per pair (two minutes of darkness for controls); birds in flight 5-85 m from the camera counted by MATLAB motion tracking
conditions: wild breeding colony, 20 nights between 14 June and 14 August 2018 (10 nights each for the spectra and interval experiments); spectra experiment at two sites (the Farm and the Neck), interval experiment at the Neck on nights with no visible moon; 81-88 light/dark pairs per colour and 86 control pairs; order of settings chosen each day with a constrained randomised design (each of six settings used 10 times over two hours, none repeated more than twice in a row); the counts are of unmarked flying adults, the authors say some birds may have passed more than once, and ages and sexes are not given. Sources were not intensity-matched: radiant flux was measured as 1.4 W (blue, 450 nm), 2.0 W (green, 540 nm), 4.3 W (red, 620 nm), 32 W (bright white) and 3.3 W (dimmed white; the Figure 1 caption gives 1.4 W), so colour and intensity are confounded and the shearwaters' spectral sensitivity was not controlled. Results: bright white -33% (95% CI 24 to 40), dimmed white -18%, blue -19.1%, green -20% (those three not significantly different from each other), red no significant overall effect and different from all other treatments, but night darkness changed the red response only: 'In other words, we counted fewer shearwaters in red light treatments during dark nights compared to moonlit nights.' (each one-SD increase in darkness increased the red effect by 22.2%, 95% CI 6 to 35); only one low red intensity was tested. Interval experiment: bright white 20 min -46%, 10 min -27%, 1 min no effect; dimmed white 20 min -33%, 10 min and 1 min no significant effect (8-10 control pairs per duration, lower power). Night-sky darkness was measured each night of the spectra experiment with a Sky Quality Meter and entered as a covariate; the interval experiment used moonless nights only. Analysis: generalised additive models with log link and negative binomial errors, random effects of pair and day and a smooth of time relative to midnight; no habituation over the experiment and no site difference in response (supplementary tables); automated counts validated against manual counts on 4 h of the 47 h 28 min of footage. The light was a T50 LED handheld torch with Cokin gel filters. The authors name neophobia as an alternative explanation and note that a torch differs from streetlights or lit vessels.

units: Hz (ABR hearing range; peak sensitivity 8-24 kHz in wild-caught and 8-32 kHz in laboratory-reared voles)
method: auditory brainstem responses to tone bursts at 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32 and 46 kHz presented from 10 to 90 dB SPL (10 dB steps, 5 dB near threshold) through TDT MF-1 speaker-couplers (1 to 24 kHz) and TDT EC-1 electrostatic speakers (32 and 46 kHz) placed in the ear canals (close-field); threshold taken by visual inspection as the lowest level at which wave I was detectable in both monaural stimuli
conditions: 53 adult or subadult prairie voles under ketamine/xylazine anaesthesia on a heating pad at 37 C: 33 laboratory-reared (16 males, 17 females, all adults over 60 days; from a long-established colony derived from wild Illinois voles in the 1980s and outcrossed among laboratories) and 20 wild-caught (10 males, 10 females; 16 adults, 4 subadults by body mass; live-trapped at the Kansas University Field Research Station, Nov 2024 to Mar 2025). The 1-46 kHz range is the span of the eight frequencies tested, so it is a tested range and not a measured limit, and the value pools the two groups. Wild-caught voles had significantly lower thresholds than laboratory-reared voles at 1, 4, 8, 16 and 24 kHz but not at 32 kHz, and there was no group difference at 2 and 46 kHz; click threshold 52 dB SPL (wild-caught) against 67 dB SPL (laboratory-reared) (Mann Whitney U, N = 50: 30 laboratory-reared and 20 wild-caught, three laboratory-reared animals absent from the click analysis without a stated reason); the origin x frequency interaction was significant (LMM, N = 53, chi2(7) = 38.72, p < 0.001); no sex differences. The speaker changes between 24 and 32 kHz (MF-1 below, EC-1 above), the boundary at which the groups' peak-sensitivity bands part and the group difference disappears. The text gives no thresholds at 1 or 46 kHz and does not say whether every animal responded there below 90 dB SPL (Table 1 not read). The paper reports no sound-attenuating chamber or ambient noise, does not mention blinding, did not control age or mating status, and notes that ABR thresholds under anaesthesia are generally 10 to 20 dB higher than behavioural thresholds in awake animals. Statistics: linear mixed-effects models with Tukey contrasts.

value: trail-following threshold of 1 fg/cm for both trail pheromone components, (3Z)-dodec-3-en-1-ol and (3Z,6Z)-dodeca-3,6-dien-1-ol, in activated workers (kept 2 h in a dish without food)
units: fg/cm of trail (lowest concentration giving active trail-following)
method: open-field Y-shaped trail-following bioassay on damp filter paper (120 degree angle between branches, moisture content 170%): a trail of extract, synthetic standard or hexane control drawn with a microlitre syringe on the 3 cm stem and/or a 5 cm branch; one termite released from a glass waiting chamber; a trail followed for more than 3.0 cm scored as active
conditions: workers from five field colonies collected at three sites around Nanjing, China, kept indoors at about 22 +/- 3 C; workers were taken at different foraging phases and 'activated' workers were held for 2 h in a Petri dish without food; each termite and each paper used once. The 1 fg/cm threshold applies to activated workers; workers taken directly in the D phase were at least ten times less sensitive to (3Z,6Z)-dodeca-3,6-dien-1-ol, and workers from the G, S and D phases preferred that component only above about 10^3, 10^4 and 10^2 fg/cm. Soldiers: 1 fg/cm for (3Z)-dodec-3-en-1-ol and 10 fg/cm for (3Z,6Z)-dodeca-3,6-dien-1-ol. The abstract gives active thresholds from 1 fg/cm to 10 pg/cm across behavioural contexts and pheromone exposure, and the two components did not act in synergy. The page text did not give the number of termites per concentration (Tables 3-7 carry the data but their rows were not returned), the full concentration series, the bioassay temperature, blinding or the order of concentrations; the applied volume is not given in the Methods. 'Active' is defined per termite (trail followed more than 3.0 cm); the paper does not say what share of termites, or what test against the hexane control, sets a threshold.

value: in a Y-maze with one lit arm, 36% of honey bees left the blue arm before the end of the test, against under 10% for UV and 23% for green
units: % of bees leaving the lit arm early
eye: foragers, whole animal (Y-maze phototaxis, UV 375 nm, blue 465 nm, green 520 nm)
method: automated three-arm Y-maze (yAPIS; arms 14 cm at 120 degrees) tracking one bee at a time in real time; coloured LEDs under the floor of an arm switched on according to the bee's position; tests of 20 s separated by 30 s, bee always starting in the dark arm
conditions: bees caught as they left colonies on the roof of the University of Konstanz, so most likely foragers of unknown age; the naive comparison is taken inside a larger conditioning design (576 bees in six groups of 96) and is tested on n = 192 (Cochran Q(2,192) = 48.32, p < 0.001; FDR-corrected post-hoc UV vs blue p < 0.001, UV vs green p < 0.001, blue vs green chi2(1,192) = 7.186, p = 0.073, so the 36% against 23% blue-green difference was not significant); separately, naive bees spent longer in UV than in blue or green and longer in green than in blue (Wilcoxon, FDR-corrected, blue vs green p = 0.017); subspecies not stated; temperature not reported; test order balanced across bees but left/right randomisation of the lit arm is not described. Intensities were calibrated to give about equal time spent, not equal photons: 64% (green), 44% (blue) and 2.4% (UV) of maximum, corresponding to 898, 1964 and 31 (x10^12, as printed) quanta/cm2/s, so UV was the dimmest in photon terms; the authors write that their settings likely left UV dimmer from the bees' perspective and that calibrating on first choice would give a longer time in UV. Training with the light (aversive pairing or exposure alone) reduced time spent in blue (blue the most labile) and did not change attraction to UV; naive bees preferred the brighter light.

value: of 28 plant-volatile materials tested, ethyl benzoate, octyl formate, methyl jasmonate and methyl dihydrojasmonate were significantly attractive
method: Y-tube olfactometer with each compound at 10 ug/uL (10 uL on 1.5 x 1.5 cm filter paper) against liquid paraffin, airflow 400 mL/min, 5 min per beetle, a choice needing more than one-third of an arm and 5 s; 60 males and 60 females per compound, each beetle tested once, arms swapped after every 5 insects and tubes replaced after every 10
conditions: screen at 10 ug/uL; the Results state that 'the rest of the compounds showed no significant attraction to either sex'; beetles making no choice in 5 min were excluded before the chi-square tests and their number is not reported; the attractions are modest per-sex chi-square results, several near P = 0.05 (for example females ethyl benzoate P = 0.047, octyl formate and methyl jasmonate P = 0.036), and 10 ug/uL was run twice with different statistics (female methyl dihydrojasmonate chi2 = 6.000, P = 0.014 in the screen, 4.414, P = 0.036 in the dose series); 56 chi-square tests in the screen with no multiple-comparison correction described; Y-tube age and mating status not stated (3 to 5 days given for EAG only); Y-tube tests at 25 +/- 1 C between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m.; laboratory colony started in 2022 from adults collected in cotton fields at the Langfang Experiment Station, Hebei, China (generation not stated), reared on Myzus persicae at 25 +/- 1 C, 65% RH, 16:8 L:D, beetles starved 24 h before tests; randomisation of test order is not described (arm swapping was the only counterbalancing). Dose series for the four active compounds (100, 10, 1 ug/uL, 60 males and 60 females each): 100 and 10 ug/uL attracted both sexes, 1 ug/uL gave no significant attraction in either sex; at 100 ug/uL only ethyl benzoate and octyl formate were stated as highly significant for females. EAG (six antennae per compound, from 3 to 5 day old adults of both sexes): octyl formate and ethyl benzoate significant at 10 and 100 ug/uL, methyl jasmonate and methyl dihydrojasmonate only at 100 ug/uL. In 1 m3 cage assays with one beetle per cage and six cages per compound, the beetle fed more on aphids on the treated plant for all four compounds in both sexes (independent-sample t tests, P from < 0.001 to 0.019). Statistics: chi-square for the Y-tube, ANOVA with Duncan's test for EAG.

value: captive house sparrow males, but not females, spent significantly more time in front of a nest box scented with hay than one scented with mouse urine
units: categorical (time in choice area, nest-box odour choice)
method: each bird tested alone in a cage with two visually identical plastic nest boxes (23 x 15 x 12 cm, 5 cm entrance), one holding 17 g of wood shavings soaked with mouse urine (bedding from ten singly housed male mice) and the other 5 g of hay, each covered with 2 g of cotton wool, with a 13 cm2 paper sheet stored 24 h in the matching material at each entrance (stimulus amounts and materials not matched; no odourless control); trials at simulated sunset in one of three visually isolated rooms at 18-20 C; video scored by an experimenter blind to subject identity and to odour position
conditions: third-generation captive-bred house sparrows (not wild-caught; wild source population not stated), all born the previous year, without breeding experience, housed in mixed-sex aviaries at the Konrad Lorenz Institute, Vienna, March to April; 15 males and 15 females tested, one female excluded for impaired exploration (14 females analysed); odour position, box identity and room randomised each trial by random number generator; 9 males and 11 females retested the next day with positions switched (repeatability R = 0.61 for males, 0.32 for females). Males: hay over mouse urine, paired t14 = 2.182, P = 0.047; females: t13 = 0.482, P = 0.638; males and females spent about 15% and 8% of total time in the choice area, and the sex difference in time (t27 = 1.542, P = 0.135) and the stimulus x sex interaction (F1,27 = 2.955, P = 0.097) were not significant, so the male preference is marginal and the sexes were not shown to differ. The measure is time spent in front of the boxes, and the authors read it as odour assessment of nest-site quality; only hay and mouse urine were offered. Each bird was caught late morning and given about four hours in an acclimatisation cage before its trial; exploration did not differ between the full-light and simulated-sunset periods.

value: tadpoles conditioned with odonate cues differed in both passive and active cell properties from water controls and from tadpoles conditioned with crayfish cues
eye: tadpole olfactory pit and mitral cells (in vivo patch-clamp; defensive behaviour in parallel tests)
method: tadpoles conditioned for five weeks (100 ml of cue water on five consecutive days then two days off, at 10-14 C) with water, crayfish-fed or odonate-fed cue water (predators fed gammarids or tadpoles); behaviour tested 48 h later in 15 x 10 x 10 cm tubs (5 min before, 1 min infusion, 5 min after, video tracked); in vivo blind patch-clamp of mitral cells with cues delivered by pressure pulse (2.7 kPa, 1.5 s) in front of the olfactory pit
conditions: eggs from six wild clutches collected in March 2016 at Parco del Ticino, Lombardy, Italy, conditioning begun at Gosner stage 25-26; 360 tadpoles (72 per treatment, two per clutch per container, two containers per treatment in each of three blocks); 9 to 14 behavioural replicates per combination; cue concentration not given beyond the preparation volumes; electrophysiology on small cell numbers (for example 5 to 6 mitral cells against 20 granule cells for baseline comparisons). Cues were from dragonfly larvae (Anax imperator, native) and crayfish (Procambarus clarkii, alien), each fed gammarids (od.1, cr.1) or tadpoles (od.2, cr.2), conditioning for five weeks from Gosner stage 25-26; recordings are from olfactory-bulb mitral cells. Passive changes were narrow: membrane capacitance differed significantly only for od.1 and the time constant was higher only for od.1. Crayfish conditioning also changed cell properties: outward current was higher than controls for all treatments except cr.2, inward current differed from controls only for od.2, and chronic exposure raised baseline firing for all groups except a marginally non-significant cr.1. Chronic exposure did not alter resting membrane potential ('Chronic larval exposure to olfactory cues did not alter the RMP of MCs.'); acute odonate cues depolarised mitral cells. The abstract reads the absence of defensive responses to non-native crayfish as non-recognition of their cues, which is the authors' inference from the recordings; against it, cr.2-conditioned tadpoles 'exhibited a clear defensive response when stimulated with the same cue.' Per-treatment mitral-cell counts are in S2 and S3 Tables only; blinding of recordings and behavioural scoring is not stated. In the Results the text says mitral cells had lower membrane resistance, while the values printed (319.8 +/- 22.4 Mohm, N = 6, against 168.5 +/- 6.8 Mohm, N = 20) show the opposite. Chronic treatment alone did not change post-stimulus activity (crayfish P = 0.16, odonate P = 0.47) whereas acute treatment did.

units: nm (UV peak of the dark-adapted ERG spectral sensitivity; a second peak at 540 nm in green)
method: electroretinograms from the left eye (microelectrode in eye and thorax) of cold-anaesthetised, immobilised females; stimuli from a 35 W xenon arc source through a scanning monochromator, 300-650 nm with 5 nm bandwidth, at a fixed 1.0 x 10^13 photons/cm2/s; response amplitude converted to sensitivity through an intensity-response function and each eye normalised by its 97.5% quantile value
conditions: 15 laboratory-colony females (Simon Fraser University colony), 3 to 4 days old; 5 per adaptation condition (45 min in darkness, green light with nominal peak 525 nm, or UV light with nominal peak 351 nm); dark-adapted eyes gave peaks at 335 nm (UV) and 540 nm (green); UV adaptation lowered sensitivity at 300-400 nm and green adaptation lowered it at 400-650 nm; the wavelength step and presentation order are not stated; stimuli were 0.5 s flashes every 10 s; no statistical test is reported for the ERG data (means with standard-error shading, n = 5 per condition), so the peaks and adaptation effects are descriptive; the colony's form (pipiens or molestus) and autogeny are not stated (adult colony at 23-26 C, 40-60% RH, 14L:10D, females blood-fed on an author's arm); no sensitivity peak was found for a blue receptor, though the authors say the green adapting light may have affected responses; the authors note the 335 nm response may also come from R1-R6, the main contributors to dipteran ERGs, not only from the central R7/R8 cells, and that the two-receptor interpretation holds 'assuming this interpretation is correct'; males not tested. Behaviour in the same paper (UV-dark inflorescences preferred) is not part of this record.
